title: Skill Disentanglement for Imitation Learning from Suboptimal Demonstrations

problem.claim: Imitation learning commonly requires many high-quality demonstrations, but collecting them is difficult and expensive; in practice, demonstration quality and quantity must be traded off.

gap.claim: Prior approaches to sub-optimal demonstrations may assume uniform demonstration optimality across time steps and may not interpret knowledge learned from noisy demonstrations.

contributions.claim: The work proposes SDIL, which evaluates and imitates demonstrations at the sub-demonstration level and encodes action primitives of varying quality into different skills.
SDIL combines a high-level skill-discovery controller with a skill-conditioned action-policy module and uses a two-phase training pipeline involving all demonstrations first and the clean set second.
SDIL uses mutual-information-based regularization and a dynamic sub-demonstration optimality estimator to promote skill-space disentanglement.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report extensive experiments in two gym environments and on a real-world healthcare dataset.
The authors report that SDIL demonstrates superiority in learning from sub-optimal demonstrations.
The authors report improved interpretability through examination of learned skills.

narrative_sequence.summary: Imitation learning trains neural agents by imitating human demonstrations in sequential decision-making tasks.
High-quality demonstrations are costly to collect, creating a practical quality–quantity trade-off.
Existing work on sub-optimal demonstrations has limitations concerning time-varying optimality and interpretation of noisy-set knowledge.
SDIL addresses these limitations through sub-demonstration-level imitation, skill disentanglement, a two-phase pipeline, regularization, and dynamic optimality estimation.
The authors evaluate SDIL across gym environments and a healthcare dataset, reporting performance and interpretability benefits.

source_observation.claim: Demonstrations can contain action primitives of varying quality within the same demonstration.

interpretation.claim: Modeling quality at the sub-demonstration level may better represent heterogeneous demonstrations than assigning one optimality level to an entire demonstration.

application.claim: For learning from mixed-quality sequential data, consider segment-level quality estimation and representations that separate reusable behaviors by quality or skill.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish that sub-demonstration-level modeling is beneficial for domains beyond the reported environments and healthcare dataset.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify quantitative results, baselines, dataset sizes, or statistical evaluation details.
The abstract does not define the exact architecture, regularization objective, or optimality estimator.
The abstract does not report computational cost, failure cases, or reproducibility details.
